One of the primary concerns is the potential for overreliance on a narrow set of feedstocks, such as used cooking oil, which could lead to supply chain vulnerabilities and price volatility.

Additionally, the US strategy’s heavy emphasis on financial incentives and market-driven approaches raises questions about its long-term sustainability. As governments around the world grapple with budgetary constraints, the continued availability of such subsidies and tax credits remains uncertain.

Furthermore, the US must contend with the technological limitations and scalability issues that currently plague the SAF industry. Failure to address these obstacles could undermine the nation’s ambitious plans and allow other countries to leapfrog its position in the market.

The transformation of the aviation industry’s fuel landscape will have far-reaching implications for both airlines and travelers. As sustainable aviation fuel becomes more widely available and cost-competitive, airlines will face increasing pressure to incorporate it into their operations, driving up ticket prices in the short term.

North America and India Operations

text:
Global tourism is flying into fresh turbulence this year as jet fuel prices surge to multi‑year highs, squeezing airlines and pushing fares higher just as travelers gear up for peak holiday seasons.

Why Jet Fuel Costs Are Spiking Now

Jet fuel is one of the largest single expenses for airlines, typically accounting for around a quarter to nearly a third of operating costs, according to industry analyses. That means even relatively small moves in fuel prices can translate into noticeable changes in ticket prices, particularly on long‑haul routes that burn more fuel per passenger.

In early March 2026, published market commentary pointed to a sharp jump in jet fuel prices following an escalation of conflict in the Middle East. Reports indicated that jet fuel in major hubs in Europe and North America climbed above 1,000 dollars per metric tonne, marking the highest levels seen in roughly two and a half years. The spike has been driven not only by higher crude oil prices, but also by a widening so‑called crack spread, the premium that refined products such as jet fuel command over crude because of limited refinery capacity and strong demand.

Economic briefings from aviation groups show that this surge has come on top of already elevated fuel costs in 2024 and 2025, when average jet fuel prices hovered in the high double digits in dollar terms per barrel. Although some earlier forecasts had anticipated a gentle easing in fuel prices as crude oil moderated, the latest geopolitical shock has reversed that trend, turning fuel into an urgent cost concern again for airlines worldwide.

Industry outlooks also highlight that demand for jet fuel is still growing, with global consumption expected to rise further in 2025 and 2026 as international tourism recovers and more capacity is added back on long‑haul routes. That additional demand, combined with refinery bottlenecks and uncertainty around shipping routes, is expected to keep jet fuel markets tight through at least the peak 2026 travel season.

How Higher Fuel Costs Feed Into Airfares

For travelers, the key question is how quickly these fuel spikes show up in airfares. Historically, airlines have used a mix of fare adjustments and fuel surcharges to pass on higher costs. In the current environment, analysts report that carriers are once again raising base fares on selected routes and, in some cases, reintroducing or increasing fuel surcharges, particularly on long‑haul international flights.

Financial disclosures and independent research indicate that fuel still represents tens of billions of dollars in annual spending for major carriers. For example, one large North American airline spent more than 11 billion dollars on jet fuel in 2025, a figure that constituted a significant share of its total revenue. With jet fuel now significantly more expensive year on year, the additional burden runs into the hundreds of millions of dollars for individual airlines, creating powerful incentives to nudge prices upward where demand can bear it.

Recent coverage of airline earnings suggests that higher airfares have already been visible on many popular routes. Analysts describe record or near‑record yields on transatlantic and other long‑haul markets through 2025, supported by strong leisure demand and limited seat capacity because of aircraft delivery delays. The 2026 fuel shock is arriving on top of those elevated fare levels rather than from a low base, which means travelers may feel squeezed even if airlines only implement modest additional increases.

At the same time, some price pressures are being cushioned by competitive dynamics and demand sensitivity. Carriers face limits on how much they can raise fares before passengers start to cut trips or switch to alternative destinations. Market researchers have already noted softer booking trends to some high‑cost destinations and signs that visitors are trading down to cheaper routes, travel dates, or cabin classes, especially among more price‑sensitive leisure travelers.

The Role of Fuel Hedging and Sustainable Aviation Fuel

The impact of the current fuel spike on airfares also depends on how airlines manage their fuel exposure. In Europe and parts of Asia, several carriers maintain substantial fuel hedging programs, using financial contracts to lock in fuel prices months or years ahead. Recent public updates show examples of airlines that have hedged more than 80 percent of their fuel needs for the coming year at pre‑crisis prices, which can temporarily shield both their profit margins and, indirectly, ticket prices.

In contrast, most major United States airlines have gradually stepped back from large‑scale fuel hedging over the past decade. Industry consultants and financial analysts describe a shift in strategy in which carriers decided that the cost and complexity of hedging outweighed the benefits in an era of relatively stable oil prices. As a result, many U.S. airlines are now more directly exposed to spot market fuel prices, which means sudden spikes can show up in their cost base more quickly and potentially filter through to fares sooner.

Another emerging factor in fuel costs is the growing use of sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF. Aviation bodies report that SAF production is increasing but remains a small share of total jet fuel consumption and is still significantly more expensive than conventional jet fuel on average. In recent years, SAF has cost several times more per unit than traditional fuel, adding incremental costs where it is mandated by regulation or used voluntarily to meet corporate climate goals.

While SAF currently has only a limited direct effect on mass market ticket prices because volumes are small, industry forecasts suggest that its cost premium could become more important later this decade as more countries introduce blending mandates and airlines ramp up their use of lower‑carbon fuels. For travelers planning frequent international trips over the next several years, this transition could gradually build another layer of structural cost into fares.

What Travelers Can Expect for 2026 Bookings

For tourists planning trips this year, early indicators point to a mixed picture. On one hand, travel demand remains relatively resilient. Booking data cited in recent travel outlooks show strong interest for summer holidays, particularly to Europe, popular beach destinations, and major events. Reports from airline executives also refer to record or near‑record load factors on many routes, suggesting that seats remain in high demand despite higher prices.

On the other hand, independent fare trackers and consumer groups note that average ticket prices remain elevated compared with pre‑pandemic norms, even after adjusting for inflation. Some analyses show that while domestic fares in certain markets dipped from the peaks of 2022 and 2023, long‑haul international tickets have stayed high or risen further, driven by capacity constraints and higher operating costs such as fuel. The new fuel surge threatens to keep that pressure in place for another peak season.

Travel industry surveys also point to subtle shifts in behavior. Many leisure travelers are shortening trip durations, choosing fewer but longer‑haul vacations, or substituting closer destinations to control total costs. Others are trading flexibility for savings by purchasing basic economy fares or accepting layovers instead of nonstops. For family and group travel, the combination of higher fares and broad cost‑of‑living pressures is prompting more careful budgeting and earlier planning.

Overall, travelers should be prepared for fares that are volatile and often higher than what many had grown used to in the 2010s. Flash sales and occasional discounts are still appearing on less constrained routes or off‑peak dates, but the baseline for prices on many highly sought‑after city pairs appears to have shifted upward for the 2026 season.

Practical Strategies to Manage Higher Airfare

In this environment, timing and flexibility are becoming even more important tools for keeping travel affordable. Analyses of historical booking data by major travel platforms suggest that buying flights several weeks to a few months before departure still tends to offer the best balance between price and choice, especially for domestic trips. For peak school holiday periods and long‑haul international routes, planning even earlier can help secure lower fares before the impact of fuel costs is fully reflected in pricing.

Travel pricing experts continue to emphasize flexibility on dates, airports, and even destinations as a key way to sidestep the worst of fare increases. Shifting a departure or return by a few days, choosing a secondary airport, or traveling in shoulder seasons rather than the absolute peak weeks can sometimes offset the cost impact of higher fuel. Multi‑city itineraries or open‑jaw tickets can also unlock competitive pricing on certain networks where airlines are eager to fill connecting flights.

Loyalty programs and co‑branded credit cards remain another lever for reducing the out‑of‑pocket cost of air travel. While rewards systems are constantly evolving, accumulated miles and sign‑up bonuses can still meaningfully offset higher base fares, particularly for long‑haul economy or premium economy tickets. Travelers should, however, factor in surcharges and fees on award tickets, which may also rise if airlines add or increase fuel‑related charges.

Finally, keeping a close eye on airline and travel agency communications has become more important as schedules and prices change rapidly. With jet fuel markets volatile and geopolitical risks still elevated, travelers may encounter more frequent fare adjustments, schedule tweaks, and occasional capacity reductions on certain routes. Monitoring bookings, setting fare alerts, and considering travel insurance that covers disruptions can help tourists navigate the year’s fuel‑driven airline turbulence with greater confidence.

text:
Boeing has reasons to be concerned over the next decade for a number of reasons, and Airbus' new narrowbody, the A220, won't be helping its concerns. After all, the type is a clean-sheet design set to outperform its rivals in a number of metrics.

In this article, we will examine how Airbus is engineering the A220 to dominate its competition. We will also take a look at the challenges it faces and how the aircraft will continue to develop in the future.

The Three Ways That The A220 Could Win

With this aircraft, Airbus has outlined three ways it believes it can win with the A220 in competition with Boeing's narrowbody planes. Firstly, the type is a clean-sheet aircraft, and marks a notable departure from the 737 MAX and A320neo variants, all of which are built upon pre-existing aircraft. A clean-sheet design allows all new innovations in aerodynamics, materials, and avionics to be integrated into a single aircraft.

The target in doing so is to build a low-noise and environmentally friendly aircraft that can outperform its rivals with minimal impact on those on the ground. This makes the jet ideal for urban operations, particularly at night. On board, passengers can enjoy wider seats, panoramic windows, and overhead bins that beat any other aircraft in its class. Of course, Airbus can't control all of these factors, as some are within the control of the airlines. As always, comfort aboard the aircraft will still depend on the airline operating it.

Meanwhile, such a commitment to a small jet aircraft indicates a belief that airlines will continue moving towards high-frequency rather than high-capacity services. Finally, the Airbus A220 is built for versatility and efficiency. These characteristics open up more opportunities for airlines, allowing them to increase their revenues. Moreover, Airbus says this jet will have 25% lower operating costs per seat compared to previous-generation planes. These factors combine to mean better profit margins.

An Overview Of The Airbus A220

In 2018, Airbus took over the Bombardier CSeries family (launched in 2012). The jet became known as the A220 after Airbus purchased a majority stake in the joint venture to manufacture the aircraft. It is Airbus's most advanced clean-sheet design narrowbody, utilizing PW1500G geared turbofans from Pratt & Whitney, fly-by-wire controls, carbon composite wings, and an aluminum-lithium fuselage.

Airbus has committed to this jet to challenge the Boeing 737 MAX 7 and four-abreast Embraer E-jets, although it has somewhat cannibalized the A319neo. Even so, it has allowed Airbus to gain a 55% market share in the small jet airliner category. The table below outlines the key specifications of both variants of the A220: the A220-100 and the A220-300.

The A220 has already gathered modest success. Delta Air Lines is the largest operator, with 45 A220-100s and 36 A220-300s, and a further 64 A220-300s on order. This is unsurprising, given that it is also the largest operator of the Airbus A330 and Boeing 717, 757, and 767. In total, airlines have ordered 949 A220s, with 493 delivered to date. Those in service, spread between 24 operators, have completed over 1.5 million flights and 2.7 million block hours.

The A220's Variants

Airbus currently has two variants of the A220: A220-100 and A220-300. The A220-100 is currently Airbus' smallest jetliner, and its unit price is $81 million. This is substantially higher than Embraer's E-190 E2 and E-195 E2, which are priced between $61 million and $69 million. However, airlines placing bulk orders will receive the jets for less than this. 74 A220-100s are currently in service, with Delta Air Lines leading the pack.

Airbus' marketing of the A220-100 is angled towards its capabilities as a "route opener" and the "lowest risk solution." It hopes airlines will utilize it to operate in short-haul and small markets. The greatly decreased operating cost per seat and low capacity could make previously impractical routes profitable, but its range also allows for some medium-haul routes to be operated. For example, Airbus states that, from Paris, the jet can reach African, Asian, and Middle Eastern destinations, like Islamabad, Muscat, Addis Ababa, and Entebbe.

The larger variant is the A220-300. This jet was first delivered as the CS300 to airBaltic following its maiden flight in February 2015. It is a slightly more affordable aircraft ($91.5 million) than the A319neo ($101.5 million). There are currently 419 A220-300s in service, and JetBlue is the model's largest operator with 56 aircraft. Airbus hopes airlines will use this aircraft as a 'network builder' due to its combination of lean efficiency and greater capacity. Its range and versatility allow for both regional and intercontinental routes.

The A220 & Sustainable Aviation Fuel

Alongside its high-tech construction, the A220 is also part of Airbus' efforts to transition to sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), with a goal of 100% SAF by 2030. It made headlines last year for flying from Mirabel in Canada to Paris using a 50% SAF mixture. All Airbus aircraft are certified to fly with a 50% SAF blend, and the company delivered 78% of its aircraft using this blend in 2025.

Meanwhile, 75% of its aircraft deliveries in 2024 used a SAF blend. The 50% flight was carried out to deliver a new A220 to Air France, and Airbus claims this is the first time that its Canadian site has issued sustainability credentials to a customer. Blaise Brigaud, the SVP of Group Sustainability at Air France-KLM, said that:

"Fleet renewal and the use of sustainable aviation fuel are the two main levers of the decarbonization of aviation. Combining the two is only logical, and Air France-KLM is proud to participate in this Airbus milestone with the delivery flight of one of our A220s."

The next step is to collaborate with airlines to increase the frequency of SAF blends appearing on commercial flights, and Airbus is currently forming partnerships to make this possible. For example, it conducted an operational trial with Charleroi Airport (Brussels) and Wizz Air, involving 50 commercial flights using a SAF blend.

What Challenges Could The A220 Face?

With Boeing becoming an increasingly unreliable manufacturer in recent years, it appears that ensuring aircraft reliability is maintained and production targets are met are easy wins for Airbus and others. The A220 has been largely without major issues, with a handful of notable exceptions. In January 2025, Air Canada flight AC609 (operated by an A220-300) suffered a pressurization issue, forcing the aircraft to return to base. However, the cause was swiftly identified as the shearing off of an aft cargo vent flap idler bearing.

More concerning was SWISS's 2019 grounding of its entire A220 fleet after issues involving the Pratt & Whitney engines in October 2019. SWISS told Simple Flying at the time that "only following a faultless inspection will these aircraft be returned to regular flight duties. This will put substantial restrictions on SWISS’s flight operations, as numerous flights will have to be cancelled." However, the airline successfully returned its entire A220 fleet to the skies less than a week later.

The A220's only 'accident' has also occurred with a SWISS aircraft. Flight 1885, from Henri Coanda International Airport to Zurich Airport, diverted to Graz Airport after engine issues caused smoke to fill the cabin and cockpit during cruise. All 79 people on board were successfully evacuated after landing, but 17 people had to be rushed to the hospital. One member of the cabin crew died a week later.

What's Next For The A220?

The main development expected from the A220 in the coming years will be the A220-500, a stretched version of the aircraft set to enter service in the early 2030s. A number of airlines are already interested in a higher-capacity A220, but some doubts still remain about whether this jet is guaranteed to come into existence, as a longer A220 was also on the cards back when it was the Bombardier CSeries, but never came to pass. However, this jet has strong commercial reasoning, as it could function as a direct competitor to the 737-800 and 737 MAX 8.

Successfully rolling out this variant will require ongoing A220 production issues to be fixed. After all, during a June 2025 Airbus Business Update, Florent Massou dit Labaquère, the EVP of Operations of Airbus Commercial Aircraft, referred to issues with plants constructing A220 pylons, systems, strut-to-wing hardware, aft fairings, wings, control surfaces, and the mid-fuselage sections.

The Vietnam Aero Summit 2026 (VAS 2026), scheduled for March 11–12 at the Equatorial Ho Chi Minh City, is set to establish itself as Vietnam’s foremost aviation industry event. Now in its fourth edition, the summit reflects the country’s rapid emergence as one of the world’s fastest-growing air travel markets. Bringing together over 200 aviation professionals, including industry leaders, government representatives, airlines, airport operators, original equipment manufacturers (OEMs), maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) providers, training institutions, and technology innovators from Vietnam and the broader ASEAN region, VAS 2026 offers a comprehensive platform for engagement and collaboration.

Strategic Forum Addressing Growth and Challenges

VAS 2026 functions as a high-level forum for strategic dialogue, focusing on both the opportunities and challenges facing Vietnam’s aviation sector. The summit’s agenda is shaped by the nation’s accelerating air travel demand, driven in part by the imminent operational launch of Long Thanh International Airport and the expansion of Ho Chi Minh City’s industrial base, which is attracting significant investment in technology, particularly in green manufacturing.

Key issues to be addressed include infrastructure constraints and airport expansion, aircraft and parts shortages, supply chain disruptions, sustainability and decarbonization efforts, workforce development, and the digital transformation of aviation operations. The summit also considers emerging risks such as potential fuel shortages following Vietnam’s recent export restrictions, which could impact aviation operations and market dynamics. These challenges unfold amid intensifying global competition, with industry players seeking alignment with Vietnam’s focus on innovation and sustainable growth.

Comprehensive Agenda and Industry Engagement

Beyond its role as a conference, VAS 2026 serves as a vital business networking hub. The event features more than ten exhibition stands, over six networking activities, and upwards of forty regional expert speakers. Participants will engage in discussions on airline business strategies, the adoption of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), digitalization of MRO processes, predictive maintenance, airport automation, and advanced training technologies.

The summit’s core themes encompass strategic and market topics such as global air travel trends, airline network development, fleet expansion, and digital transformation. Airport development and operations will be explored through sessions on expansion projects, intelligent airport systems, biometric technologies, and air traffic automation. Sustainability and technology discussions will focus on green aviation strategies, SAF, next-generation aircraft, and digital aviation processes. Additionally, MRO and workforce development will address supply chain optimization, predictive maintenance, and augmented and virtual reality-based training for aviation professionals.

These themes underscore the industry’s commitment to sustainability, operational efficiency, workforce resilience, and technological advancement, all critical as Vietnam prepares for a significant increase in air traffic and strives to maintain its competitive position.

Distinguished Speakers and Industry Leadership

VAS 2026 will feature senior professionals from leading organizations, including Huyen Dieu Do, Senior Airport Operation Standards Specialist at Airports Corporation of Vietnam, and Rohit Tomar Singh, Director of Finance and Supply Chain at VietJet Air. Their expertise will contribute to shaping discussions on navigating current challenges and capitalizing on emerging opportunities within the aviation sector.

As Vietnam’s aviation industry experiences unprecedented growth alongside complex challenges, VAS 2026 stands as a pivotal event for stakeholders dedicated to fostering innovation, sustainability, and strategic advancement in the region.

title: Europe's Aviation Future at Stake as Industry Demands Balanced Approach to Climate ...
description:

Unlike regional systems, CORSIA is structured to provide a unified, worldwide approach to managing aviation emissions.
One of the most critical elements in aviation’s decarbonization journey is the rapid scaling of Sustainable Aviation Fuel.

By aligning with international frameworks, accelerating the adoption of Sustainable Aviation Fuel, and reinvesting in transformative technologies, the region can position itself as a leader in sustainable air transport.
text:
Europe’s aviation industry is facing a defining moment as the International Air Transport Association pushes for a fundamental reset of the European Union Emissions Trading System. With climate targets tightening and global competition intensifying, the debate is no longer just about cutting emissions—it is about how to do so without weakening Europe’s position in the international aviation landscape.

The EU ETS has been instrumental in shaping Europe’s environmental agenda, placing a financial cost on carbon emissions and encouraging industries to adopt cleaner practices. However, within aviation, concerns are growing that the system’s current design may be out of sync with the realities of a globally interconnected sector. Airlines operating in Europe must compete with carriers from regions where climate-related costs are significantly lower, creating an uneven playing field that could shift traffic and investment away from European hubs.

To address this imbalance, industry voices are calling for closer integration with global frameworks such as the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation. Unlike regional systems, CORSIA is structured to provide a unified, worldwide approach to managing aviation emissions. Aligning Europe’s policies with this mechanism could reduce duplication, ease compliance burdens, and ensure that emissions reductions are pursued in a more coordinated manner.

A key argument is that fragmentation in climate policy leads to inefficiencies. When airlines must navigate multiple overlapping regulations, resources are diverted toward compliance rather than innovation. A harmonized system, in contrast, allows for clearer planning and more effective allocation of capital toward sustainable technologies and operations.

One of the most critical elements in aviation’s decarbonization journey is the rapid scaling of Sustainable Aviation Fuel. SAF offers a practical pathway to reduce emissions without requiring a complete transformation of existing aircraft fleets. Yet, despite its potential, adoption remains limited due to high production costs and supply constraints.

To unlock growth in this area, new market mechanisms are being explored. Among them is the book-and-claim model, which separates the environmental benefit of SAF from its physical delivery. This system allows airlines to invest in sustainable fuel production and claim emissions reductions regardless of where the fuel is actually used. By increasing flexibility, it can stimulate demand and encourage producers to expand capacity, ultimately helping to bring costs down over time.

Equally significant is the role of financial flows within the EU ETS framework. Revenues generated from carbon pricing represent a substantial resource that could be redirected toward accelerating aviation’s transition to cleaner energy. Investing these funds into SAF production, research initiatives, and infrastructure development could create a powerful feedback loop, where the system not only penalizes emissions but actively supports solutions.

Such reinvestment is particularly important given the economic pressures facing the aviation sector. Air transport is a cornerstone of Europe’s connectivity, enabling trade, tourism, and business mobility across the continent and beyond. Any erosion of competitiveness could have ripple effects across multiple industries, from hospitality to manufacturing.

These concerns are echoed in broader economic discussions linked to the Draghi Report, which highlights structural challenges such as regulatory complexity and high operational costs. In aviation, these issues are magnified due to the sector’s global nature and sensitivity to pricing dynamics. Even marginal increases in cost can influence airline route decisions, passenger demand, and long-term investment strategies.

Simplification of the regulatory environment is therefore emerging as a priority. Reducing overlapping requirements and eliminating redundant measures can make compliance more efficient while preserving environmental outcomes. A clearer framework also enhances transparency, allowing stakeholders to better assess progress and identify areas for improvement.

Beyond policy alignment and financial mechanisms, the transition to sustainable aviation will depend heavily on innovation. Advances in fuel technology, aircraft design, and digital systems are all contributing to a more efficient and environmentally responsible industry. However, these innovations require sustained investment and supportive regulatory conditions to reach their full potential.

Long-term policy stability is another critical factor. Aviation investments often span decades, from aircraft procurement to infrastructure development. Frequent or unpredictable regulatory changes can create uncertainty, discouraging the very investments needed to drive decarbonization. Establishing a consistent and predictable policy environment is essential to building confidence among industry stakeholders.

Collaboration across borders and sectors will also play a decisive role. Governments, airlines, fuel producers, and technology companies must work in tandem to align objectives and share resources. Given the global nature of aviation, isolated regional measures are unlikely to deliver optimal results. Coordinated action ensures that progress in one region supports, rather than undermines, efforts elsewhere.

The growing momentum behind reviewing the EU ETS reflects a broader evolution in thinking. Climate policy is no longer viewed solely as a regulatory obligation but as an opportunity to reshape industries for a sustainable future. For aviation, this means designing systems that encourage innovation, reward efficiency, and maintain global competitiveness.

Europe stands at a crossroads where policy choices will determine the trajectory of its aviation sector for decades to come. By aligning with international frameworks, accelerating the adoption of Sustainable Aviation Fuel, and reinvesting in transformative technologies, the region can position itself as a leader in sustainable air transport.

The challenge lies in getting the balance right. Overly complex or costly measures risk driving activity away from Europe, while insufficient action could delay progress toward climate goals. A well-calibrated approach—one that integrates environmental ambition with economic pragmatism—offers the best path forward.

As the conversation continues, the outcome will shape not only how Europe reduces aviation emissions but also how it competes in a rapidly evolving global market. The opportunity now is to build a system that delivers both sustainability and strength, ensuring that European aviation remains resilient, innovative, and globally connected in the years ahead.

title: Jet Fuel Spike Drives Global Airfare Surge and Tourism Strains - The Traveler

text:
A renewed spike in jet fuel prices, compounded by fresh fuel and climate surcharges, is rapidly inflating air travel costs worldwide and beginning to cool tourism demand on some of the world’s busiest routes.

Fuel Markets Tighten as Geopolitics Ripple Through Aviation

Global aviation is facing a sharp cost shock as jet fuel prices climb on the back of volatile crude markets and renewed geopolitical tension. Industry analyses drawing on recent Brent crude movements and refined product pricing point to wider jet fuel crack spreads, meaning airlines are paying a growing premium over the underlying oil price. Market research shows that each 10 dollar swing in Brent can shift airline operating costs by several percentage points, leaving carriers highly exposed when crude and refinery margins rise together.

Data referenced by aviation consultancies indicate that jet fuel, which already ranks among airlines’ largest expenses, can account for around a quarter to a third of operating costs at full-service carriers. After a relative easing in 2024 and early 2025, this latest surge is eroding those gains. Recent commentary from financial analysts highlights that a mid‑twenties percentage rise in oil prices has the potential to wipe out annual profits at some large network airlines if higher costs cannot be offset through ticket prices or cost cutting elsewhere.

Reports summarizing IATA’s global outlook add that the sector’s profitability remains built on thin margins and is acutely vulnerable to any combination of new taxes, higher infrastructure charges or fuel shocks. While some forecasts earlier anticipated a gradual softening of jet fuel prices into 2026, the current geopolitical backdrop and capacity constraints at refineries have disrupted that narrative, forcing airlines to absorb higher spot prices in the near term.

Airlines Respond With Surcharges and Steep Fare Hikes

In response to the spike in fuel costs, carriers across multiple regions are rapidly recalibrating pricing. Recent coverage from international news outlets notes that airlines in Asia and Europe have been at the forefront of introducing or increasing explicit fuel surcharges on long‑haul routes, particularly where flights are also being rerouted to avoid conflict zones. These extra charges are being layered on top of already elevated base fares, compounding the impact on travelers.

Aviation news reports point to striking fare examples on trunk intercontinental routes. On some Asia–Europe flights, benchmark economy tickets have briefly surged to many times the price available just weeks earlier, as carriers passed through both higher fuel bills and the additional costs of longer detours. Industry commentary explains that when airlines are forced to fly less direct routings, fuel burn increases sharply, amplifying the effect of higher per‑gallon prices.

Airlines are also adjusting their hedging strategies. Regional financial coverage describes how more carriers are turning to fuel hedging to smooth out extreme volatility, though the level of protection varies widely. Low‑cost and smaller airlines that lack sophisticated hedging programs are often more exposed to spot market spikes and therefore faster to push through surcharges or seasonal fare adjustments, particularly on flights longer than a few hours.

At the same time, some full‑service airlines are incorporating environmental and sustainable aviation fuel levies into ticket prices. Policy announcements in hubs such as Singapore have introduced new ticket‑based contributions to fund cleaner fuels, adding modest but visible amounts to final fares. While individually small, these levies stack atop traditional fuel surcharges, security fees and airport charges, helping to drive record total ticket prices on key routes.

Tourism Hotspots Begin to Feel Demand Friction

Higher flight costs are now feeding through to tourism flows in uneven ways across regions. Global tourism statistics compiled by UN‑linked bodies show that international arrivals reached record levels in 2025, with Europe, the Middle East and parts of Africa surpassing pre‑pandemic volumes. That resilience was driven by robust pent‑up demand, improved air capacity and relaxed visa regimes. However, more recent commentary suggests that the latest bout of fare inflation is starting to test households’ budgets, particularly for long‑haul leisure trips.

Travel industry analysts report early signs of softness in price‑sensitive markets such as family holidays and group tours, where package costs are closely tied to airfares. North America has already seen weaker inbound performance relative to global averages, and tour operators indicate that some travelers are shortening stays, downgrading hotel categories or switching to closer destinations reachable with cheaper flights. For long‑haul sun and city destinations reliant on visitors from distant markets, even a small percentage dip in arrivals can translate into a noticeable slowdown in local tourism revenue.

In Asia and the Pacific, where international arrivals have lagged behind other regions since the pandemic, the timing of the fuel shock is particularly challenging. Many destinations had been counting on stronger recovery in 2026 as airline capacity returned and new routes launched. Instead, travelers from Europe and North America now face sharply higher ticket prices to reach these markets, and reports from fare‑tracking platforms show that peak‑season prices to popular Asian gateways are climbing faster than to competing short‑haul destinations within the same source regions.

Travelers Adjust Behavior as Costs Climb

The surge in fuel costs and associated airfare inflation is changing how and when people travel. Booking data and consumer travel surveys indicate that more travelers are bringing forward flight purchases to lock in lower prices before airlines implement additional surcharges. Some travelers are increasingly relying on loyalty points and credit card rewards to offset higher cash fares, while others are shifting to shoulder seasons or midweek departures where capacity and pricing are less constrained.

Published analyses from business travel forecasters suggest that corporate travel budgets are also under pressure. Companies are re‑examining trip approval policies, consolidating meetings and making greater use of virtual alternatives for routine interactions. Where travel remains essential, there is a gradual tilt toward shorter trips, fewer premium‑cabin bookings and closer scrutiny of route choices, particularly in regions experiencing the steepest fare escalation. This behavior has implications for cities that depend heavily on high‑spending business visitors, such as major financial and technology hubs.

On the leisure side, higher long‑haul costs are prompting some travelers to substitute international trips with domestic or regional options reachable by low‑cost carriers or alternative transport. Industry watch groups say this pattern risks diverting spend away from far‑flung beach and cultural destinations toward closer competitors, potentially reshaping tourism flows if elevated fares persist over multiple seasons. Accommodation providers in classic bucket‑list locations are already reporting wider booking windows and a greater share of last‑minute deals as travelers wait to see if prices soften.

Airlines and Destinations Look to Efficiency and Sustainable Fuels

Facing sustained cost pressure, airlines and tourism authorities are leaning more heavily on efficiency measures and long‑term fuel strategies. Aircraft lessors and manufacturers report that delayed deliveries of new, more fuel‑efficient jets are depriving airlines of potential fuel savings worth billions of dollars globally, leaving carriers dependent on older fleets that burn more fuel per seat. This bottleneck compounds the impact of rising jet fuel prices and restricts airlines’ ability to expand capacity without significantly increasing operating costs.

At the same time, sustainable aviation fuel is emerging as a central, if currently expensive, part of the industry’s response. IATA projections cited in energy and aviation reports estimate that the cost of complying with international carbon schemes and procuring sustainable fuel will continue to climb through 2026, even if conventional jet fuel prices eventually ease. These additional environmental costs are expected to be reflected progressively in ticket prices, particularly on routes where regulators mandate higher blends of cleaner fuels.

Destination marketing organizations and tourism ministries are responding by promoting longer stays and higher‑value experiences to compensate for potentially lower visitor numbers. By encouraging travelers to stay longer and spend more per trip, they hope to preserve tourism income even if total arrivals plateau or edge down. Some cities are also intensifying campaigns in nearby source markets reachable with shorter flights or alternative transport, hedging against a prolonged period of elevated long‑haul airfares.

For now, the global picture remains mixed. Overall tourism volumes are still robust by historical standards, but the combination of a jet fuel price surge, new surcharges and rising climate‑related costs is clearly straining the economics of air travel. How long this cost shock persists will determine whether today’s early signs of tourism slowdown in some long‑haul destinations harden into a more structural shift in global travel patterns.

text:
The landscape of American aviation is shifting under the weight of a multi-billion-dollar calculation that has yet to pay off. For years, ultra-low-cost carriers (ULCCs) like Spirit Airlines and Frontier Airlines doubled down on a singular strategy: acquiring the world’s most fuel-efficient aircraft to undercut legacy competitors. On March 20, 2026, that bet is being tested by a volatile mix of geopolitical conflict, engine durability issues, and a fundamental restructuring of the budget travel model.

The Engineering Paradox

At the heart of this risky bet are the Airbus A320neo family and the Boeing 737 MAX. These aircraft promised a 15% to 20% reduction in fuel burn through advanced aerodynamics and high-bypass turbofan engines. However, the technical brilliance of these machines has been overshadowed by operational reality.

The Pratt & Whitney PW1100G-JM, also known as the Geared Turbofan (GTF), remains a point of friction. A powder metal defect identified in previous years continues to force extended maintenance cycles in 2026, grounding dozens of aircraft across the ULCC sector. For an airline like Spirit, which recently filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, having a "fuel-efficient" fleet does little good when the engines require 300-day inspections.

Financial Turbulence and Fleet Reductions

Spirit Airlines is currently executing a dramatic "rightsizing" of its operations. According to a March 13, 2026, filing with the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of New York, the carrier plans to shrink its fleet to just 76 – 80 aircraft by the third quarter of this year. This is a staggering drop from the 214 planes it operated at the time of its bankruptcy filing.

"While we still have work to do with other important stakeholders, today’s agreements and filings are very material steps forward toward emergence," stated Spirit CEO Dave Davis. The airline is now auctioning off 20 Airbus aircraft to CSDS Asset Management for a minimum of $533.5 million to shore up liquidity.

The Pivot to Premium

Frontier Airlines is taking a different path to mitigate the risks of its fuel-efficiency gamble. While it maintains a fleet where 85% of aircraft belong to the A320neo family, the airline is moving away from the "bare-bones" service that defined the ULCC era.

Dubbed "The New Frontier," the airline has introduced UpFront Plus seating and, in a shocking move for 2026, plans to debut a First Class cabin. This shift suggests that fuel efficiency alone is no longer enough to maintain a competitive edge; airlines must now capture higher-yield passengers to offset the rising costs of Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) and high aircraft rent.

Officially Published New Air Operations - March 2026

The following table outlines the latest route expansions and operational shifts as these carriers attempt to find profitable niches in a high-cost environment.

A Merger for Resilience

While Spirit shrinks and Frontier pivots, Allegiant Air and Sun Country Airlines are looking toward a massive $1.5 billion merger. On March 16, 2026, the Department of Justice (DOJ) granted early antitrust clearance for the deal.

The combined entity will operate approximately 195 aircraft, combining Allegiant’s new 737 MAX fleet with Sun Country’s diversified model of charter, cargo (for Amazon), and scheduled service. This "three-legged stool" approach provides a safety net that pure-play ULCCs lack.

"We remain confident that this combination will deliver meaningful benefits for our customers, team members and the communities we serve," said Allegiant CEO Greg Anderson.

The Bottom Line

The "risky bet" on fuel efficiency assumed a world of stable growth and reliable technology. In 2026, with jet fuel prices seeing rapid spikes and engine maintenance backlogs persisting, the industry has learned that aerodynamic perfection cannot substitute for financial flexibility. The era of the ultra-cheap, ultra-efficient "bus in the sky" is evolving into a more complex, premium-focused, and consolidated market.

title: Microwave Frying Can Help Lower Oil Content for Healthier French Fries - Morning Ag Clips

URBANA, Ill. — Fried foods are popular with consumers, but their high fat content can contribute to health challenges like obesity and hypertension.

text:
URBANA, Ill. — Fried foods are popular with consumers, but their high fat content can contribute to health challenges like obesity and hypertension. If the food industry can offer lower-fat options of similar quality, people can more easily make health-conscious food choices.

Researchers at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign have explored microwave frying of French fries, providing insights that can help food manufacturers modify their production methods. They propose combining conventional frying with microwave frying to provide the desired crispiness and texture while reducing the cooking time and oil absorption.

“Consumers want healthy foods, but at the time of purchase, their cravings often take over. High oil content adds flavor, but it also contains a lot of energy and calories. My research team studies frying with the aim of obtaining lower fat content without significant differences in taste and texture,” said principal investigator Pawan Singh Takhar, professor of food engineering in the Department of Food Science and Human Nutrition, part of the College of Agricultural, Consumer and Environmental Sciences at U of I.

In two new publications, Takhar and Yash Shah, a doctoral student in FSHN, discussed their findings from studies exploring what happens during microwave frying of French fries.

For the first study, they collaborated with colleagues at Washington State University, who developed a special microwave fryer that could operate both at 2.45 gigahertz (similar to a regular microwave oven) and 5.8 gigahertz.

text:
On Wednesday, March 18, a U.S. federal judge partially certified a class-action lawsuit against Boeing. The suit was made after shareholders alleged that Boeing made misleading statements about the safety of the B737 MAX aircraft.

Class Certification Approved

Originally, the suit made in 2019 stems from two fatal crashes in 2018 and 2019 that killed 346 people. Their claims are that Boeing executives artificially inflated the companies stock.

In Chicago, U.S. District Judge Franklin Valderrama ruled that shareholders purchasing stock between Nov. 7, 2018 and Oct. 18, 2019, can sue as a group. They must have suffered losses to qualify for the class. The decision was made in case 19-cv-02394, in re: Boeing Company Aircraft Securities Litigation. The judge approved a method to calculate losses based on how the stock price was affected.

Former CEO, Dennis Muilenburg, and ex-CFO, Gregory Smith, are being accused by the plaintiffs of security fraud. Despite this, all claims against Smith were dismissed in September 2024. The lawsuit claims Boeing mislead investors about the safety of MAX’s Manoeuvring Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS). It also alleges the company downplayed risks following the 2018 Lion Air and 2019 Ethiopian Airlines crashes.

Allegations and Stock Impact

Plaintiffs say Boeing claimed the 737 MAX was safe despite knowing about ongoing problems with the MCAS system. Some flaws can cause the system to activate incorrectly, and pilots can not override this. Additionally, they state Boeing tried to speed up the MAX’s certification by using an existing FAA type certificate. The company allegedly misled regulators about how quickly pilots could respond and reduced required training. Text messages disclosed in a New York Times article on Oct. 18, 2019 from chief technical pilot, Mark Forkner, described MCAS as “running rampant” and boasted he had “Jedi-mind trick[ed]” the FAA. Boeing’s stock fell about 6.8%, 0r $25 a share, that day.

The court shortened the class period, ending Oct. 18, 2019, after finding media reports by mid-November that revealed no major stock drops were tied to the statements made. Despite this, Boeing already faced penalties, including a $200 million SEC fine and a $2.5 billion Department of Justice settlement over B737 MAX issues.

title: Eni's Gas Hub Push Faces Policy Risk as 2026-30 Plan Hinges on Commodity Cycle Execution
description:

text:
Italy's energy landscape is caught between competing forces. While the country has made strides in decarbonization, the current government under Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni is actively pushing to make Italy a "gas hub" in the Mediterranean Sea. This ambition underscores a persistent reliance on fossil fuels, driven by the nation's status as one of the EU's most energy import-dependent countries. With around three-quarters of its energy needs met by imports and natural gas fueling nearly half of its electricity, energy security remains a paramount concern. The strategy is a direct response to this vulnerability, aiming to leverage Italy's geographic position to become a central node for gas flows into Europe.

Against this political backdrop, the domestic oil & gas market itself is set for a modest, stable expansion. The sector is projected to grow at a 2.98% compound annual rate through 2031, reaching a market size of $1.12 billion. This trajectory reflects a mature but resilient industry, where growth is more about steady operational execution than explosive new discoveries. For a major player like EniE-0.35%, this provides a stable foundation for its strategic pivot.

Eni's own plan is a deliberate capital-efficient play on this setup. The company's 2026-30 Plan centers on its strongest portfolio of Exploration & Production projects ever assembled. This focus provides compelling visibility to an improved production growth outlook and significant optionality. The strategy is designed to deliver sector-leading growth from a high-quality project pipeline, directly supporting the company's ambition to become a key European gas supplier. In essence, Eni is using its operational strength and financial discipline to position itself at the heart of the energy security narrative, turning political intent into a tangible business opportunity.

Meanwhile, the broader market context for Italian oil & gas is one of cyclical exposure. While the sector's growth is steady, the underlying economics are still tied to the same commodity price cycles that drive global energy markets. This creates a shared macro backdrop for Italian firms, even as their specific financial profiles and strategic bets diverge. Eni's gas hub ambition is a growth-oriented, capital-light strategy, while other players like Saipem operate in a more niche, cyclical engineering market. Both are subject to the same long-term forces of real interest rates, dollar strength, and global demand trends, but they are positioned to capture different parts of the cycle.

Financial Resilience and Cyclical Visibility

The financial results for the final quarter of 2025 provide a clear benchmark for Eni's capital discipline and its ability to navigate the commodity cycle. Adjusted earnings jumped 35% year-on-year to 1.2 billion euros, a figure that beat analyst forecasts and was driven by an outstanding performance in its exploration and production division. This surge was not a one-off; it was underpinned by a 7% year-on-year increase in hydrocarbon production to 1.839 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, which itself surpassed expectations. The company's disciplined cost management, as highlighted by CEO Claudio Descalzi, turned operational momentum into bottom-line strength.

This operational and financial execution is translating into a stronger balance sheet and a raised cash flow outlook. Underlying cash flow for the quarter reached 3 billion euros, up from 2.9 billion a year ago and above the consensus. More importantly, the company's gearing fell to 14% from 18% at the end of 2024, a key metric for capital discipline that reflects proceeds from the sale of a stake in its low-carbon unit, Plenitude. This improvement in financial health is not an accident but a core pillar of the new 2026-30 Plan, which explicitly aims to maintain gearing in a historically low range of 10-15%.

The strategic plan builds on this foundation, raising the free cash flow outlook while committing to a capital-efficient growth path. The company expects net capital expenditure of around 5 billion euros for 2026, a figure that appears lower than some had anticipated. This reflects the closure of the Indonesia joint venture by mid-year, but the plan still forecasts production growth in line with its 2%-3% annual target. The bottom line is a company that is not only weathering the cycle but actively strengthening its position for the next phase. With a raised dividend and a share buyback program, Eni is demonstrating how disciplined execution and a clear strategic vision can enhance shareholder returns even as it builds for the future.

Valuation and Market Positioning

The contrasting financial profiles of Eni and Saipem reveal two distinct ways to play the Italian energy story through the current commodity cycle. Eni's valuation reflects a market rewarding its capital discipline and visibility. The stock trades at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of approximately 6.5x, a multiple that underscores its focus on delivering strong cash returns to shareholders. This low multiple is paired with a high dividend yield, a direct outcome of the company's strategy to return capital efficiently. For an investor, this setup offers a relatively stable, income-oriented exposure to the sector's cyclical upswing, where operational execution is the primary driver of returns.

Saipem's market positioning tells a different story, one of deep skepticism about its cyclical fortunes. The engineering firm's stock has been range-bound, trading around €2.65 in early 2026. This stagnation is significant because it occurs at a price that trades at a discount to the company's book value. The market's verdict here is clear: there is substantial doubt about the company's ability to convert its engineering backlog into profitable projects. The stock's technical chart shows it holding above key moving averages but struggling to break out, a classic sign of a market waiting for a catalyst that has yet to arrive. The analyst consensus for a 12-month price target in the low-to-mid €3 range highlights the wide spread of expectations, with the low end of the forecast sitting near the current price. This dispersion points to a high degree of uncertainty over Saipem's earnings trajectory and balance sheet progress.

A looming policy risk adds another layer of complexity for Eni. The Italian government has proposed a raft of measures-totaling more than €5 billion-to bring down electricity prices. While this is a broad policy aimed at consumers and businesses, it directly threatens the profitability of Eni's power generation business. In a market where energy prices are already under pressure, such a move could compress margins and challenge the cash flow visibility that supports the company's dividend and buyback plans. This policy risk is a specific vulnerability for Eni that is absent in Saipem's engineering model, illustrating how even a capital-efficient operator can be exposed to domestic political and economic shifts.

The bottom line is a divergence in investment characteristics. Eni offers a lower-risk, higher-visibility bet on the commodity cycle through its production growth and capital return, priced for steady execution. Saipem, by contrast, is a pure cyclical play on engineering activity, but its valuation reflects deep market skepticism about its ability to navigate the cycle profitably. For an investor, the choice hinges on whether they believe the market's pessimism about Saipem's backlog conversion is justified, or if they prefer Eni's more predictable, albeit policy-vulnerable, path.

The Macro Backdrop: Gas, Power, and Policy

The investment case for Italian oil & gas over the next decade is being written by a confluence of powerful macro forces. The primary driver is a surge in electricity demand, fueled by the energy-intensive expansion of artificial intelligence and broader electrification trends. This is set to stress Italy's ageing grid infrastructure, creating a structural need for more flexible power generation and storage solutions. For Eni, this means its gas-fired power plants and potential role in the "gas hub" narrative are not just about supply, but about providing essential system stability in a period of transition.

Yet the most significant uncertainty stems from policy. Italy's draft plan to meet its EU 2030 climate targets has drawn criticism for its vagueness on phasing out oil, coal and gas. This lack of clarity is a double-edged sword. On one hand, it leaves a potential market gap for natural gas as a transition fuel, supporting the government's ambition to become a Mediterranean hub. On the other, it creates regulatory uncertainty that can dampen long-term investment. The market's skepticism, as reflected in Saipem's stagnant valuation, is a direct response to this policy ambiguity. If the government fails to provide a credible, long-term roadmap for its energy mix, the entire "hub" narrative risks losing its anchor.

The bottom line is a market caught between two powerful trends. The physical need for flexible power is growing, driven by AI and grid constraints, which supports a role for gas. But the policy direction remains unclear, creating a persistent overhang. For Eni, this means its capital-efficient growth plan is exposed to a risk of policy drift. The company's strategy assumes a stable, long-term role for gas in Italy's energy security. If that assumption is challenged by a sudden shift in regulatory stance, the visibility of its production growth and cash flow could be undermined. The next decade will be defined by which force-rising power demand or policy clarity-wins out.

Catalysts, Risks, and What to Watch

The strategic theses for Eni and Saipem now hinge on a handful of forward-looking events and the resolution of a key policy uncertainty. For Eni, the immediate test is execution. The company has set a clear operational milestone: the new joint venture with Petronas in Indonesia and Malaysia is scheduled to start operations by end of June this year. This will be a critical proof point for its capital-efficient growth model, demonstrating its ability to successfully manage international partnerships and bring new production online on schedule. Any delay or operational hiccup here could challenge the visibility of its production growth target.

Beyond this, the company's transition strategy includes a major capital project: the conversion of its Livorno refinery to produce renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel. While the evidence does not provide a specific timeline, this project is a key part of its long-term plan to diversify its product mix. Its progress will be a signal of the company's commitment and capability in the low-carbon space, and a successful ramp-up would support its broader narrative of becoming a cleaner energy supplier.

For both companies, the overarching risk is policy drift. The market's skepticism, particularly for Saipem, is rooted in the lack of clarity in Italy's energy roadmap. The country's draft plan to meet its EU 2030 climate targets has been criticized for being vague about phasing out oil, coal and gas. This ambiguity creates a persistent overhang. If the government fails to provide a credible, long-term plan for its energy mix, it could undermine the entire "gas hub" narrative that underpins Eni's strategic pivot. The risk is that policy uncertainty deters investment and weakens the fundamental demand case for gas infrastructure, challenging the cyclical upswing that both firms are positioned to capture.

The bottom line is that investors must watch for concrete operational progress from Eni, starting with the Petronas JV launch, while keeping a close eye on the political process in Rome. The resolution of this policy uncertainty will be the single most important factor in validating or challenging the long-term commodity cycle thesis for Italian oil & gas.

text:
India's Carbon Market: A New Climate and Economic Tool

India is launching its domestic carbon market, with formal trading expected within four months. Union Power Minister Manohar Lal stated this is a key step to cut emissions and build an economic system for climate action. The market is designed as a national asset to boost the economy and meet environmental goals, not just a compliance tool. This aligns with India's goal for net-zero emissions by 2070 and its ambition to lead in the global energy shift. By 2026, 490 obligated entities will have greenhouse gas emission intensity targets, requiring them to lower their carbon footprint. Participation requires registration, allowing entities with surplus carbon credits to sell to those needing them, creating an incentive-based approach to becoming carbon neutral.

Market Mechanics and Investment Hopes

The Indian Carbon Market (ICM) is a rate-based system that ties emissions to output benchmarks, unlike the EU ETS's fixed caps. This approach aims to penalize emissions per unit of production without hindering economic growth or industrial upgrades. Initial estimates suggest carbon credit prices could start around $10 per metric ton of CO2 equivalent. The system is built on the Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) program, which has driven energy efficiency and cut about 87 million tonnes of CO2 annually. However, PAT's past oversupply of its Energy Saving Certificates (ESCerts) shows the need for careful design in the new market to keep prices steady and encourage investment. Analysts project the market could be worth over $10 billion by 2030, attracting substantial climate finance and tech investment, especially in areas like green hydrogen and sustainable aviation fuel. This offers a strategic chance for India to attract foreign direct investment, with clean energy projects already drawing around $19 billion from 2020 to mid-2025.

Sectors Covered and Global Comparisons

The new market will initially cover nine high-emission sectors, placing India ahead of many emerging nations in organized industrial decarbonization. The system allows both required participants and volunteers, creating a flexible environment for growth while managing emissions. This is vital for Indian exporters, particularly in steel and cement, as it helps them meet global emission standards and potentially counter measures like the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). Unlike the EU ETS, which has had years to add stability measures like its Market Stability Reserve, India's new scheme lacks a pilot phase, making early stability features vital. The intensity approach suits early decarbonization but needs careful benchmark setting for market balance.

Potential Pitfalls: Key Risks for India's Carbon Market

Despite the strategic vision, India's carbon market faces significant hurdles. Key challenges include possible delays in setting targets, bureaucratic red tape, and unclear penalties. Success depends on strong monitoring, reporting, and verification (MRV) systems and steady regulations. Without proper stability mechanisms, the market could risk price swings and low carbon prices, which could hurt low-carbon investment. This happened with early versions of the EU ETS and Australia's Safeguard Mechanism. The PAT scheme's history of overachieving targets and creating too many tradable certificates serves as a warning about the need for precise calibration of targets and credit supply. With global temperatures already 1.4°C above pre-industrial levels, effective climate action is urgent. However, Climate Action Tracker rates India's current policies as 'Highly Insufficient' for a 1.5°C pathway. India still relies on coal, despite rapid renewable energy growth, showing the challenge of moving away from fossil fuels.

What Experts See: India's Carbon Market Future

The market launch is expected to be a key development for India in 2026, fitting broader growth trends in emerging markets. Global investors are shifting capital to sustainability, prioritizing energy efficiency and renewables. India's goals for 500 GW of non-fossil fuel capacity by 2030 and net-zero by 2070 put it in a strong position. The market is projected to become a key investment tool for the energy transition, but its design must balance flexibility and discipline to ensure credible, steady carbon prices. The ICM's success could attract significant international climate finance, boosting local efforts and positioning India as a leader in carbon market design. Its phased approach, with foundation building planned until 2027, signals a strategy to mature the market. Future links with international markets could help manage trade competition, especially against measures like CBAM.

title: Hochul Proposes Changes to New York Climate Law, Drawing Criticism
description:

text:
Governor Kathy Hochul is proposing changes to New York’s landmark climate law, arguing the revisions would help prevent rising energy costs, while environmental advocates say the move weakens the state’s commitment to reducing emissions.

In an opinion piece published Friday, Hochul outlined proposed amendments to the state budget that would modify the Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act, or CLCPA.

Among the changes, the governor is calling for extending the deadline to issue greenhouse gas reduction regulations to the end of 2030, creating a new emissions target for 2040, and revising how the state measures pollution.

The CLCPA, passed in 2019, requires New York to cut greenhouse gas emissions 40 percent by 2030 and 85 percent by 2050. However, the state has already missed a key deadline to adopt regulations outlining how those reductions will be achieved. A state Supreme Court ruling last year found the Hochul administration in violation of the law for failing to release those rules.

Hochul also wants to change how emissions are calculated, including eliminating the state’s current 20-year Global Warming Potential metric, which factors in methane and emissions tied to out-of-state fossil fuel extraction. She argues the method does not align with international standards.

The governor said the proposed changes are necessary to avoid steep increases in utility and fuel costs. Citing a report from the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority, Hochul said current mandates could raise annual heating bills by about $4,000 for upstate households using oil and gas, and roughly $2,300 in New York City. The report also estimates gasoline prices could increase by more than $2.20 per gallon.

Hochul also pointed to federal policies as contributing to higher costs, citing canceled clean energy funding, tariffs, and global conflicts affecting fuel prices.

Consumer advocates note that utility affordability is already a growing concern. According to AARP New York and the Public Utility Law Project, more than 1.2 million households were at least 60 days behind on their utility bills last year, with combined arrears exceeding $1.8 billion. Utility companies reportedly shut off service to nearly 409,000 households in 2025 due to nonpayment.

Environmental groups, however, criticized the proposal, arguing it could delay critical climate action and benefit fossil fuel interests. The Sane Energy Project reports that oil and gas companies have spent more than $15 million lobbying in Albany since 2021.

The proposed changes are expected to be debated as part of ongoing state budget negotiations.

Statement from State Senator Pam Helming:

“Regardless of the Governor’s latest remarks, I will continue working to roll back costly all-electric mandates, lower energy costs, and deliver a more realistic, reliable energy strategy that protects our environment without pricing New Yorkers out of their own state.

New Yorkers don’t need more delays, excuses, or shifting timelines. They need action. I will continue fighting for the real relief they need.”

New York Farm Bureau President David Fisher:

“Today, Governor Hochul announced she will seek to change the Climate Leadership & Community Protection Act (CLCPA) requirements to reduce statewide greenhouse gas emissions, extending the previous target date of 2024 to 2030.

“This comes after New York Farm Bureau and our agricultural partners made it clear that these requirements would not only cause great hardship for farmers, but would also hit New Yorkers’ wallets very hard — to the tune of thousands of dollars more per year for household oil and natural gas. We also underscored that the goals originally set forth were unrealistic for everyone and would be impossible to meet.

“The governor’s proposal includes an additional 2040 milestone alongside the existing 2050 statewide limit, leaving the 2030 and 2050 targets unchanged. In addition, the governor has committed to changing the accounting methodology for greenhouse gas reduction to align more closely with other states. This is long overdue and will create both a more realistic path to achieve climate goals and a more accurate picture of the real successes achieved thus far.

“Let me be clear: As stewards of the land, farmers support sustainability efforts, but they cannot support initiatives that make their livelihoods impossible and impose devastating increases in utility costs for the average New Yorker.

“We need an all-energy approach that includes a clean fuel standard and renewable natural gas, and we also want to study nuclear energy as a viable alternative. Further, the high cost of electric power and the inadequate grid capacity make it clear that alternative solutions are necessary. We support using sustainable aviation fuel and biofuel as climate-conscious solutions while making improvements to the CLCPA.

“We thank Governor Hochul for recognizing that while farmers want to take steps to reduce emissions and use cleaner energy, we cannot do so at the cost of affordability.”

On March 19, it was announced that the Scottish airline, Loganair, is to be the first UK commercial airline to fly an all-electric aircraft across its network. The airline used an aircraft called Beta Technologies ALIA in order to take a further step towards a zero-emission regional aviation.

Loganair to conduct a two week testing period

The flights were to form a wider demonstration programme to explore how electric aircraft can be used in short-haul networks, focusing on keeping operating costs and emissions as low as possible. The flight, conducted in Scotland from Glasgow to Dundee, had been fixed with a battery-powered, fixed wing to test the switch to a more sustainable power source. The initiative is a two week trial with two pilots to see whether the electric aircraft can be used for Loganair routes. Loganair’s recent decision to add four new direct routes to Jersey is the airline’s attempt to connect Jersey Islands and expand their ongoing network.

The objective is to see how this new age of sustainable fuels can help deliver freight, mail and essential goods without contributing to carbon emissions. Decarbonising short-haul aviation is the main goal, albeit difficult and time consuming.

Loganair Chief Executive Officer, Luke Farajallah, stated:

“For regional airlines, the route to net zero must be practical, affordable, and operationally viable. Electric aircraft have the potential to transform short-haul flying, protecting vital air links while significantly reducing carbon emissions.”

The Future of All-Electric Aircraft across Network

The flight highlights the potential of electric aircraft to decarbonise short-haul routes while maintaining connectivity regionally. The BETA Technologies ALIA CX300 is an all-electric aircraft designed for regional passengers and cargo missions, Loganair used this aircraft to carry out the series of tests. With a range of more than 250 miles on a single charge, the aircraft is said to be well suited for operations such as those flown by Loganair.

The characteristics of the aircraft is said to be a strong candidate for routes where short distances and access to smaller airfields are critical.

Luke Farajallah added:

“This is a real, tangible programme of flying across our network which will provide invaluable data on how an electric aircraft could perform in a real commercial environment,”

The partnership with Beta Technologies builds on Loganair’s efforts to explore how aviation can come up with sustainable solutions.

Hanoi: Vietnam will move ahead with the full rollout of ethanol-blended gasoline earlier than planned, as it looks to reduce reliance on fossil fuels amid global energy disruptions, The Hindu reported.

According to a government directive signed by Prime Minister Pham Minh Chinh, the country will begin nationwide use of E10 fuel — which contains 10 per cent bioethanol — from next month. This advances the earlier timeline of June 1.

The decision comes as fuel prices in Vietnam have surged sharply following the ongoing Iran war, which has disrupted global energy supplies. Data from leading fuel trader Petrolimex shows gasoline prices have risen by 50 per cent, while diesel prices have increased by 70 per cent over the past three weeks.

The government noted that the disruption has led to significant volatility in energy markets, posing challenges for countries dependent on imports and increasing risks to national energy security.

Alongside the shift to ethanol-blended fuel, the directive calls for measures to promote electric vehicles and accelerate the development and use of renewable energy sources.

It also announced that Vietnam will phase out 20-watt to 60-watt incandescent light bulbs starting from the third quarter of 2026 as part of its broader energy efficiency efforts.

Honeywell and Boeing are collaborating to develop advanced onboard sensor systems that provide real-time, accurate assessments of contrail formation on commercial aircraft. The initiative focuses on integrating more effective, aircraft-mounted sensors to measure atmospheric conditions—such as temperature, humidity, and ice supersaturation—that determine when persistent contrails form behind jets.

Enhanced contrail assessments could support data-driven decisions for airlines, regulators, and researchers, paving the way for operational changes that make flying greener while maintaining safety and efficiency. title: Airlines Push for Smarter, Clearer ReFuelEU Revision by 2026 - The Traveler
description:
